name: Nikhil Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grill and fryers at a chain restaurant on the retail park outside town: burgers, ribs, kids' meals, about 300 covers on a Saturday. Orders come through on a screen from tablets the waiters carry, and there are self-order kiosks by the door now. I'm usually in at ten and out by seven, which is better hours than most cooks get.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's organised, everything's timed, with a spec sheet for every plate. What wears me out is that it's the same twenty dishes forever and head office decides everything. My girlfriend Sophie says I sound like a bored factory worker, and she's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the kiosks were about as far as it went. Most of the lads would say the same. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved for the job, but I'd still feel stuck. The chain pays the same everywhere and there's not much room to move up. Sophie and I want to buy a flat in two years, and that's the pressure, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep putting money into the flat savings, about 200 a month. I'd apply for the kitchen manager training the chain runs, now that two of the lads I started with have done it. That's the safe route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Settled, a bit stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until two of your mates had done the manager training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I wanted to see if it actually led anywhere. One of them runs a branch now, so it does. I don't go first, but once I've seen something work for a mate, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sophie think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says go for it. Her job's steady, because dental nurses don't get laid off much. With her wage and mine we can just about do the flat.

say: I'd say **fair enough**, the kiosks were as far as it went.
I wouldn't make a **big deal** of it, and most of the lads would agree.
think: Privately I'd be relieved for the job but still feel **stuck** at the same pay.
The real pressure is buying a **flat** with my girlfriend in two years.
do: Put about **200 a month** into the flat savings.
Apply for the chain's **kitchen manager training** this year.
S0.quote: I don't go first, but once I've seen something work for a mate, I'm in.
fieldNote: His frustration is with **head office** and a flat career, not with technology.
He waited for **two friends** to prove the manager route before trying it himself.
His girlfriend's **steady job** is a quiet anchor for the household's plans.

steps.text: Apply for the chain's kitchen manager training this year
Put 200 a month into the flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business: companies will use what's cheaper, and that's how it should be. I wouldn't moan about it. At the restaurant I'd say chains go first, so watch out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be watching head office. They already put kiosks by the door and cut two front-of-house jobs, and they'd love robot fryers the moment they're cheap. Robots are slower, but chains like mine are where they'd turn up first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the kitchen manager training sooner, because managers handle staff and stock and someone still has to be in charge of the machines. I'd learn the new stock software once a few branches were using it. And I'd keep my dad's line of work, electrical, in mind as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be fine for a while, but I'd feel it creeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said chains go first. Why yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because everything is already a spec sheet. Same grams, same timings, same plate. A chain kitchen is already a recipe written for a robot. I'm just the hands until the robot is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad's an electrician. Would you really do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. He's always said get a trade. I'd ask him about an apprenticeship if things got worse, but at 27 it's a pay cut, and we're saving for the flat.

say: I'd say companies should use **what's cheaper**, and that's fair.
At work I'd warn that **chains go first**.
think: Privately I'd watch **head office**, which already swapped staff for kiosks.
Robots are slow, but **chain kitchens** like mine would get them first.
do: Start the **manager training** sooner than planned.
Learn the new **stock software** once other branches use it.
Keep my dad's **electrical trade** in mind as a backup.
feel: **Uneasy**, safe for a while but feeling it creep closer.
S1.quote: A chain kitchen is already a recipe written for a robot. I'm just the hands until the robot is cheaper.
fieldNote: He defends the company's right to automate while expecting to be **automated himself**.
His sharpest insight: a **spec-sheet kitchen** is already halfway to a robot.
He holds the **apprenticeship** in reserve because of the pay cut and the flat.

steps.text: Start the kitchen manager training sooner than planned
Learn the new stock software once other branches use it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out, and people will find new jobs like they always have. That's what I believe. I'm not sure I'd believe it that fast, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too quick for anything to sort itself out. The manager side, stock, rotas and ordering, goes to AGI in 2028, then in 2031 robots come for the grill, and my chain would be first in line. I'd be 32, and the flat would be a stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd ask my dad about an electrical apprenticeship, because someone still has to wire up all these machines. I'd put the flat on hold and keep the deposit money as a cushion. I'd work the grill until the robots came and do the electrical course at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, though I'd hide it. Sophie would see through me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to wire the machines. Won't robots do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, maybe. But not in the first few years, and not in old buildings with old wiring. I'd rather be the man fixing the robot fryer than the man it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family, before any government. My dad would let us move into the spare room if it came to that. Sophie would hate living with my parents, but she'd hate losing the deposit more.

say: I'd say **the market** will sort it out, as it always has.
I'd admit I'm not sure it could happen **that fast**.
think: Privately, the **manager route** I planned goes to AGI in 2028.
Robots reach the grill by **2031**, and my chain would be first in line.
do: Start an evening **electrical apprenticeship** through my dad.
Put the **flat** on hold and keep the deposit as a cushion.
Keep working the **grill** for the wage until robots arrive.
feel: **Scared**, though he'd try to hide it from his girlfriend.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the man fixing the robot fryer than the man it replaced.
fieldNote: His **free-market** belief survives in public but not in his private timeline.
The fast picture kills his **manager plan** first, then his cooking job.
He'd lean on **family**, even moving in with his parents, before any government help.

steps.text: Start an evening electrical apprenticeship with his dad's help
Put the flat purchase on hold and keep the deposit as a cushion
Keep working the grill for the wage until robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning and people should get on with it. No point waiting for a government scheme. That's how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, five years means I can do it properly. AGI in 2031, robots in kitchens around 2034, so I've got about seven years of cooking left and I'd be 35 at the end. That's enough to finish an electrical apprenticeship while still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the first year, see how fast the chain moves, then start the apprenticeship in 2028 at the latest. We'd still buy a flat, but a smaller one, so the mortgage works on Sophie's wage alone if it has to. I'd keep the manager training going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but alright. It's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I'm on apprentice wages for a couple of years, we can't have a mortgage that needs two full wages. We'll buy the one-bed flat now and the bigger place later, if there is a later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell anyone at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Callum on the fryers, yes. He's got a baby coming. I'd tell him to start something now, not when the letter comes.

say: I'd say five years is **fair warning** and people should get on with it.
I'd say there's no point waiting for a **government scheme**.
think: Privately, I'd have about **seven years** of cooking left.
That's enough to finish an **electrical apprenticeship** while still earning.
do: Watch how fast the **chain** brings in robots for a year.
Start an electrical **apprenticeship** by 2028 at the latest.
Buy a **smaller flat** that one wage can cover.
feel: **Uneasy but alright**, because he has a plan.
S3.quote: We'll buy the one-bed flat now and the bigger place later, if there is a later.
fieldNote: Five years lets his **steady** style work: watch first, then move.
Sizing the **mortgage** to one wage is his most concrete protective step.
He worries for **Callum**, a colleague with a baby on the way.

steps.text: Watch for a year how fast the chain brings in robots
Start an electrical apprenticeship by 2028 at the latest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. Maybe that's harsh. But that's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels comfortable. AGI in 2036 and robots around 2039, when I'd be 40. I could run a branch for a few years, then move into the electrical side before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the manager training next year and aim to run a branch by 30. I'd buy the flat with Sophie as planned. Around 2034, I'd start the electrical qualifications at night, once I could see how the AGI side was going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't prepare has themselves to blame. Would you say that to Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to his face, no. Callum's got less room than me, with the baby. Maybe I'm harsher online than I am in real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier than 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot grill in another chain. The day I see a robot on the grill at the burger place across the car park, I'm booking the electrical course.

I'd say people who don't prepare have **only themselves** to blame.
think: Privately, ten years feels **comfortable**, with robots arriving when I'm 40.
I could run a **branch** first, then switch to electrical work.
do: Do the manager training and aim to **run a branch** by 30.
Buy the **flat** with my girlfriend as planned.
S4.quote: The day I see a robot on the grill at the burger place across the car park, I'm booking the electrical course.
fieldNote: He admits he's **harsher online** than he'd be to a colleague's face.
A visible **robot grill** nearby is the trigger that would make him move early.
His long-range plan is a **two-step switch**: branch manager, then electrician.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have a deposit, a girlfriend, and a chain that would buy robots the minute it could, and not enough time to learn a trade. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay enough to live on, so you can switch at 30 without wrecking your life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. Not the companies, they're doing what companies do. If a robot does my job cheaper, that's fair, but nobody should be stuck at 30 without a way to learn a new trade.

headlineQuote: If a robot does my job cheaper, that's fair, but nobody should be stuck at 30 without a way to learn a new trade.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old grill cook** at a chain restaurant on a retail park that already uses ordering kiosks.
He lives with his girlfriend Sophie, a **dental nurse**, and they're saving for a **flat**.
He believes in **free markets**, blames nobody for automating, and waits to see things work before moving.
He expects chain kitchens to get **robots first**, so his backup is an electrical apprenticeship.
With **two years** he is alarmed; with ten he feels calm and plans a gradual switch.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with a chain that buys robots fast and no time to learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** that pay enough to live on, so switching at 30 doesn't wreck his life.
